# P13.2: source audit and proved partial results

**Status: incomplete for the unchanged original P13.2.** This document does not establish an intrinsic sufficient condition for solvability on every normal polarized affine cone. In particular, it does not prove existence for every finite-energy probability measure on the invariant carrier for an irrational Reeb field. The results below are partial mathematical arguments and a source-application audit, not a completed solution or a verification verdict.

Only the four supplied public primary-paper caches were used. Their exact versions are Wu21 = arXiv:2106.13395v2, Wu24 = arXiv:2406.13684v1, BJ22 = arXiv:1801.08229v4, and BJ23 = arXiv:2307.01697v1. References to LF lines use one-based inclusive ranges of the literal UTF-8 extract split by `split('\n')`. Form feeds are retained and do not count as new LF lines. `source-extracts/source-provenance.json` embeds the literal statements and relevant proof bodies, their ranges, all supplied PDF/extract hashes, and application checks. The eight supplied PDF/extract hashes match. No book proof, other campaign, generated draft, or additional primary paper was read.

## 1. Actual objects and probability normalization

Let $X=\operatorname{Spec}R$ be a normal affine cone of dimension $n$, with good effective torus action $T$, homogeneous decomposition $R=\bigoplus_\alpha R_\alpha$, cone vertex $o$, maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, and Reeb field $\xi$ in the open Reeb cone. Put

$$X_0=\{v:v(\mathfrak m)=0\},\qquad K=X_0^T.$$

Write $\rho=\varphi_\xi$. Using homogeneous generators $f_j$ of $\mathfrak m$,

$$\rho(v)=\max_j\frac{-v(f_j)}{\langle\xi,\alpha_j\rangle},\qquad \rho^+=\max\{\rho,0\}.$$

In particular $\rho|_{X_0}=0$. The source volume convention is

$$V_\xi=\operatorname{vol}(\xi)=\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{n!}{m^n}\sum_{\langle\xi,\alpha\rangle\le m}\dim R_\alpha.$$

The genuine mixed operator and energy are, with the source's $d'd''$ convention,

$$\operatorname{MA}_\xi(\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_{n-1})=V_\xi^{-1}d'd''\varphi_1\wedge\cdots\wedge d'd''\varphi_{n-1}\wedge d'd''\rho^+,$$

$$E_\xi(\varphi)=\frac{1}{nV_\xi}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\int(\varphi-\rho)(d'd''\varphi)^j\wedge(d'd''\rho)^{n-1-j}\wedge d'd''\rho^+.$$

Thus the transverse dimension is $n-1$, there are $n$ terms in the energy sum, and the energy denominator is $nV_\xi$, not $(n+1)V_\xi$. The radial factor is part of the measure and cannot be discarded. Wu21 Definition 2.4 (LF 205–211), Wu24 Theorem 2.12 (LF 321–332), and Definition 4.1/Proposition 4.2 (LF 522–554) fix these conventions. The mixed measures are probabilities; $E(\rho)=0$ and $E(\varphi+c)=E(\varphi)+c$.

For a finite positive Radon measure $\nu$ of mass $m$, translating any continuous psh potential gives

$$E(\varphi+c)-\int(\varphi+c)d\nu=E(\varphi)-\int\varphi d\nu+(1-m)c.$$

Consequently finiteness of this dual supremum forces $m=1$. This is a direct check on the actual affine-cone normalization, not an imported projective convention. For $a>0$, $V_{a\xi}=a^{-n}V_\xi$, $\rho_{a\xi}=a^{-1}\rho_\xi$, and

$$\operatorname{MA}_{a\xi}(a^{-1}\varphi)=\operatorname{MA}_\xi(\varphi),\qquad E_{a\xi}(a^{-1}\varphi)=a^{-1}E_\xi(\varphi).$$

These identities follow by scaling all $n$ current factors. They concern a single Reeb ray.

## 2. Torification, the model carrier, and corrected density

Define torification by

$$\tau(v)(f)=\min_{\alpha:f_\alpha\ne0}v(f_\alpha),\qquad f=\sum_\alpha f_\alpha.$$

Here is a construction that also verifies multiplicativity. The action homomorphism sends $f$ to $\sum f_\alpha\chi^\alpha$ in $R[M]$. Pass from $R$ to the fraction field of $R/\ker v$, equipped with its induced valuation, and extend that valuation to the Laurent polynomial ring by the Gauss rule, giving every character value zero. The minimum-of-coefficients rule is multiplicative: reducing terms of minimum valuation gives nonzero Laurent polynomials over the graded residue domain, whose product is nonzero. Pull back along the action homomorphism. This gives precisely the displayed formula, including the case where all coefficients vanish in $R/\ker v$. It proves that $\tau(v)$ is a semivaluation.

Homogeneous evaluations are unchanged. The criterion in Wu21 Lemma 2.8 (LF 269–297), proved there by an invertible character matrix, implies that $\tau(v)$ is $T$-invariant and fixes invariant semivaluations. Every evaluation $\tau(v)(f)$ is a finite minimum of continuous extended-real evaluations, so $\tau$ is continuous. The homogeneous generators of $\mathfrak m$ show $\tau(X_0)\subset K$ and $\tau^2=\tau$. Thus $K$ is a closed compact retract of $X_0$.

For completeness, $v(\mathfrak m)=0$ forces $v(g)\ge0$ for every $g\in R$: if $v(g)<0$, choose $h\in\mathfrak m$ with finite value and apply $v$ to $g^rh\in\mathfrak m$ as $r\to\infty$. This contradicts $\inf_{\mathfrak m}v=0$. The bounded-semivaluation space is a closed subset of the compact product $[0,+\infty]^R$, with one evaluation coordinate for every element of $R$. The link is its closed subset given by the equation $\min_jv(f_j)=0$ for finitely many generators of $\mathfrak m$. This also verifies compactness without identifying the entire punctured analytic cone with the link.

Every homogeneous FS test factors through $\tau$. Uniform limits and decreasing pointwise limits preserve this identity, so all genuine psh and finite-energy potentials factor through $\tau$ on $X_0$. The same holds for differences of continuous potentials.

**Model carrier.** Wu21 Corollary 5.7 states explicitly that the unnormalized mixed model measure has finite support on $T$-invariant points of $\{\rho=0\}$ (LF 1049–1054). Its proof uses vanishing of the top homogeneous wedge off the vertex, tropical facet calculations to obtain locally discrete support, compactness to make the support finite, and torus invariance of the current to make that finite support a $T(k)$-set. The final argument is valid: a divisible abelian group has no nontrivial finite quotient, since a finite abelian group of exponent $e$ has $eG=0$. Hence the action on the finite support is trivial, and every supporting point is invariant (LF 1092–1200). This proves support in $K$, rather than merely setwise torus invariance of a diffuse measure. The sentence in the preceding proof that a Hessian “has to be zero” should mean singular: linearity in the Reeb direction makes its determinant zero, not the whole Hessian zero.

There is an additional literal defect in the auxiliary Wu21 Lemma 5.8 (LF 1058–1091): it sums currents on the *full* hyperplanes $V_i=\{v_i\cdot x=0\}$, although the zero set of the maximum contains only active boundary facets. For $\psi(x,y)=\max\{x,y\}$ a test form near $(0,1)$ sees the $x=0$ term on the left and no point of $\{\psi=0\}$ on the right. Thus the lemma cannot be applied literally. In the boundary computation, one must use the oriented facets of the polyhedral region, restricted to $\{v_i\cdot x=0,\ v_j\cdot x\le0\ \forall j\}$, with redundant facets removed. On a compact subset of the relative interior of such a facet the active linear form is unique, so gradients of locally uniformly converging convex smooth approximants converge to its gradient; this follows by bounding derivatives between the two finite-difference quotients on a small line segment. Gradients are locally bounded by the same convexity estimate. Intersections of facets have lower dimension and give zero facet integration measure, allowing exhaustion of facet interiors. This supplies the needed boundary-trace restriction in the local discrete-support argument. No equality involving the full hyperplanes is used here, and no general mass coefficient is imported from that defective lemma. The normalized carrier application also uses Wu24's independently printed Theorem 2.12, under exactly its normal-cone, Reeb, and homogeneous-FS hypotheses.

Wu24 Theorem 2.12 already prints $X_0^T$ as the model carrier. For continuous potentials use model approximation at fixed $\xi$, and for finite-energy potentials use the decreasing-net continuity of the genuine mixed operator in Wu24 Theorem 6.3. Every approximating measure has mass one on closed $K$. A weak limit has the same property: for each nonnegative continuous function vanishing on $K$, its integral is zero throughout and at the limit; Radon regularity then gives zero mass to $X_0\setminus K$. Hence every genuine finite-energy output is a probability on $K$.

**Corrected density theorem.** Let $D_\xi$ denote restrictions to $K$ of differences $\phi-\psi$, where $\phi,\psi\in\operatorname{CPSH}(a\xi)$ for some $a>0$. Then $D_\xi$ is a real vector lattice containing constants and is uniformly dense in $C(K)$.

To prove the vector-lattice assertion, use the same-ray addition and scaling rules of Wu24 Proposition 3.3. If $u=\phi_1-\phi_2$ at $a\xi$ and $v=\psi_1-\psi_2$ at $b\xi$, their sum is a difference at $ab/(a+b)\xi$, and

$$\max\{u,v\}=\max\{\phi_1+\psi_2,\psi_1+\phi_2\}-(\phi_2+\psi_2).$$

Both terms on the right have that same polarization. Multiplication by a positive scalar follows from rescaling the polarization; negatives follow by interchanging the terms. Constants come from $\rho+c-\rho$.

For separation, two different invariant semivaluations differ on some nonzero homogeneous $f\in R_\alpha$. The weight is nonzero, since the zero-weight part is the ground field for a good cone. Put $d=\langle\xi,\alpha\rangle>0$. For sufficiently large finite $A$ the function

$$u_{f,A}=\max\{(-v(f)+A)/d,\rho(v)\}-\rho(v)$$

separates the two points. On $K$ it is $\max\{(A-v(f))/d,0\}$; this also separates a finite evaluation from $+\infty$. The first maximum is a genuine FS function because the reference generators are retained. The real lattice Stone–Weierstrass theorem now proves the density assertion.

Wu24 Theorem 3.5 literally prints density in $C(X_0)$ (LF 416–417), and its proof assumes two different points differ on a homogeneous function (LF 434–435). That assumption holds on $K$, not on the full link. The same correction applies to Theorem 3.6: its tests can approximate continuous equivariant functions that factor through torification. Also, the printed algebraic formula for the maximum at LF 424–432 is not the valid lattice identity above.

**Explicit full-link counterexample.** Take $X=\mathbb A^2$, $T=(\mathbb G_m)^2$, and $\xi=(1,1)$. Let $w$ be evaluation at $(1,1)$ as a semivaluation, and let $v_{\rm triv}$ be the generic trivial valuation. Both belong to $X_0$. Every nonzero homogeneous monomial has value zero at both, so $\tau(w)=v_{\rm triv}$. But $w(x-y)=+\infty$, whereas $v_{\rm triv}(x-y)=0$. Thus they are distinct and $w\notin K$. All psh tests agree at these points. Since each FS function has its maximum on $X_0$ at the trivial valuation, $E(\phi)\le\phi(v_{\rm triv})$; pass to decreasing approximants to obtain this for finite-energy functions. Therefore

$$E^\vee(\delta_w)=E^\vee(\delta_{v_{\rm triv}})=0.$$

Nevertheless $\delta_w$ cannot be an output, by the carrier result. This does not refute the target problem, whose target domain is $K$. It proves that unrestricted full-link dual energy cannot determine the genuine output measure. The continuous function $e^{-v(x-y)}$ also directly separates the two points while all homogeneous tests agree.

## 3. Energy signs and literal normalization defects

For $\phi,\psi\in\mathcal E^1(\xi)$ the correct inequalities are

$$\int(\phi-\psi)\operatorname{MA}(\phi)\ \le\ E(\phi)-E(\psi)\ \le\ \int(\phi-\psi)\operatorname{MA}(\psi).\tag{1}$$

For continuous potentials, the successive mixed terms in the energy difference decrease with the number of $\phi$ factors, by integration by parts and the Hodge inequality. Their average lies between the first and last terms. For finite-energy potentials approximate both decreasingly; Wu24 Theorem 6.3 gives continuity of all involved integrals and energies. This proves (1), with no arbitrary non-psh variation.

Equivalently, along an admissible segment the first derivative is $\int u\operatorname{MA}(\phi_t)$ and the second derivative is

$$\frac{n-1}{V_\xi}\int u\,d'd''u\wedge(d'd''\phi_t)^{n-2}\wedge d'd''\rho^+\le0.$$

Wu24 prints an incorrect intermediate second-derivative formula at LF 595–600, omitting the $d'd''u$ factor and the $n-1$ coefficient; the correct formula appears immediately afterwards at LF 605–610. Its Hodge proposition at LF 485 names the equivariant difference space, although its proof assumes the invariant difference space. Our use is only for $u=\phi-\psi$, which is invariant.

Wu24 Proposition 7.3's proof prints the first inequality in (1) with the opposite direction (LF 1247–1249). Repairing that direction gives, for every genuine output,

$$E^\vee(\operatorname{MA}(\phi))=E(\phi)-\int\phi\operatorname{MA}(\phi)<\infty.\tag{2}$$

Indeed (1) bounds $E(\psi)-\int\psi\operatorname{MA}(\phi)$ above by the right side of (2), and equality is obtained at $\psi=\phi$. Mixed finite-energy integrability makes the right side finite. The resulting energy duality in Proposition 7.3 is consistent; the printed supporting inequality is not.

There are also genuine normalization conflicts in Wu21. Its Lemma 3.16 gives $S=\frac n{n+1}\widetilde S$ for the truncated-degree filtration invariant, while Corollary 5.14 identifies the genuine energy with projective energy. Theorem 5.15(1) nevertheless prints $E^{\rm NA}=S$. For the homogeneous filtration weight $\chi(f_\alpha)=c\langle\xi,\alpha\rangle$ on a polynomial cone, the FS potential is $\rho+c$, so the probability-normalized energy is $c$. Counting monomials in the truncated simplex gives $S=cn/(n+1)$, whereas the equal-degree invariant is $\widetilde S=c$. This disproves a literal application of $E=S$ with those definitions. It agrees with the $(n+1)/n$ factor occurring in Wu24 Proposition 7.4. No general equality in that proposition's irrational approximation is inferred here; its printed conclusion is only an upper bound.

Likewise Wu21 Theorem 6.3 (LF 1442–1447) prints

$$E^{\rm NA}(\chi)=\frac1{(n+1)V_\xi}\int_{P_\xi}\widetilde\chi\,d\lambda,\qquad \lambda(P_\xi)=V_\xi.$$

For the same constant-on-the-slice weight $\widetilde\chi=c$ this is $c/(n+1)$, contradicting $E(\rho+c)=c$. The formula, with its literal stated measure convention, is not applied. This constant-shift check does not determine every correction to that section; it suffices to rule out using its displayed normalization unchanged.

## 4. Intrinsic necessary test and finite-energy approximations

On the actual carrier define

$$E^\vee_\xi(\mu)=\sup_{\phi\in\mathcal E^1(\xi)}\left(E_\xi(\phi)-\int_K\phi\,d\mu\right).$$

The following intrinsic **necessary**, not sufficient, test uses only homogeneous FS functions:

$$\mu\text{ is a probability on }K,\qquad\sup_{\phi\in\mathcal H(\xi)}\left(E_\xi(\phi)-\int_K\phi\,d\mu\right)<\infty.\tag{3}$$

Its equivalence to finite dual energy is proved next; its sufficiency for solving the equation is not proved.

**Radon decreasing-net lemma.** If $f_i$ are continuous and decrease to an upper semicontinuous $f$ on compact $K$, then $\int f_i d\mu\downarrow\int f d\mu$, allowing $-\infty$. To verify the net issue, use the regularity formula $\int f d\mu=\inf_{g\in C(K),\,g\ge f}\int g d\mu$ for bounded-above usc functions, with truncation for $-\infty$. For any such $g$ and $\epsilon>0$, the open sets $\{f_i<g+\epsilon\}$ increase and cover $K$. Compactness supplies one index covering $K$. Consequently $\inf_i\int f_i\le\int g+\epsilon$. Taking infima and letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves the lemma. This is the compact-carrier argument behind BJ22 Lemma 7.17, without an unjustified countable monotone-convergence theorem for arbitrary nets.

Approximate any $\phi\in\mathcal E^1$ decreasingly by FS $\phi_i$. The energy converges to $E(\phi)$ by Wu24 Proposition 5.10, and the preceding lemma gives convergence of target integrals even when the limit is $-\infty$. Hence the supremum over FS equals the supremum over $\mathcal E^1$. If it is finite, every finite-energy potential has finite integral, because otherwise its own contribution to the supremum would be $+\infty$. Formula (2) proves that every output satisfies (3).

This argument gives target integration continuity for decreasing FS approximation of a *fixed* potential. It does not prove continuity for arbitrary weakly convergent energy-bounded potentials, as needed in an attainment argument.

**A repaired elementary mixed-integrability bound.** Let $\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_{n-1}$ be continuous psh functions nonpositive on $K$, and put $B=\max_i\{-E(\phi_i)\}$. Then

$$\int_K\phi_0\operatorname{MA}(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{n-1})\ge-\frac{n^{n+1}}{(n-1)!}B.\tag{4}$$

To prove it put $\bar\phi=n^{-1}\sum_i\phi_i$. Concavity gives $E(\bar\phi)\ge-B$. Every mixed term in its energy sum is nonpositive. Keeping just the last term therefore gives the valid inequality

$$E(\bar\phi)\le\frac1n\int\bar\phi\operatorname{MA}(\bar\phi).$$

Since $\bar\phi\le\phi_0/n$, positivity gives an upper bound $n^{-2}\int\phi_0\operatorname{MA}(\bar\phi)$. In the expansion of $\operatorname{MA}(\bar\phi)$, the term with one copy of each $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{n-1}$ has coefficient $(n-1)!/n^{n-1}$. Multiplication by $\phi_0\le0$ permits dropping all other terms for an upper bound. Thus

$$-B\le E(\bar\phi)\le\frac{(n-1)!}{n^{n+1}}\int\phi_0\operatorname{MA}(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_{n-1}),$$

which is (4). Wu24 Lemma 6.4's proof has an incorrect $E(\bar\phi)\le\int\bar\phi\operatorname{MA}(\bar\phi)$; the extra $1/n$ in the repaired bound matters. The displayed definition of $J$ there also omits the $-E$ term and the energy sum has an incorrect upper index. Formula (4) is a repaired continuous estimate with an explicit, nonoptimal constant. Passing from it to arbitrary weak target integration is not justified by this bound alone.

## 5. What maximizing sequences actually yield

Let $\mu$ satisfy (3). The finite supremum has an FS maximizing sequence $\phi_j$ by the defining property of a supremum. Set

$$\Delta_j=E^\vee(\mu)-E(\phi_j)+\int\phi_jd\mu\longrightarrow0.$$

The fixed-Reeb estimates already suffice to prove that this sequence is Cauchy for $I$, modulo constants. Here are the details, avoiding a realization assumption. Write $Q_n$ for a quasi-triangle constant:

$$I(\phi,\psi)\le Q_n\bigl(I(\phi,\theta)+I(\theta,\psi)\bigr).$$

For $\theta=(\phi+\psi)/2$, the $J\ge I/n$ bounds give

$$E(\theta)-\tfrac12E(\phi)-\tfrac12E(\psi)=\tfrac12J_\theta(\phi)+\tfrac12J_\theta(\psi)\ge\frac{I(\phi,\psi)}{2nQ_n}.$$

The integral terms cancel because $\theta$ is the midpoint. The left side is also

$$\tfrac12\Delta_\mu(\phi)+\tfrac12\Delta_\mu(\psi)-\Delta_\mu(\theta)\le\tfrac12\bigl(\Delta_\mu(\phi)+\Delta_\mu(\psi)\bigr).$$

Therefore

$$I(\phi_j,\phi_k)\le nQ_n(\Delta_j+\Delta_k)\longrightarrow0.\tag{5}$$

This uses only Wu24's fixed-ray $I$–$J$ bounds and quasi-triangle inequality, whose proofs use the invariant differences and Hodge forms. Taking $\psi=\rho$, with $\Delta_\mu(\rho)=E^\vee(\mu)$, also gives

$$J_\rho(\phi_j)\le(n-1)Q_n\bigl(\Delta_j+E^\vee(\mu)\bigr).\tag{6}$$

Finally, Wu24 Lemma 7.7 gives that $\operatorname{MA}(\phi_j)$ is $I^\vee$-Cauchy. This statement concerns images of actual potentials only. It does **not** identify any weak limit with $\mu$, or prove that the Cauchy sequence has a limit in the genuine $\mathcal E^1/\mathbb R$. No closure of unknown outputs is proposed as an image characterization.

The source defines $I$ and $I^\vee$ as quasi-pseudometrics at this stage. Its literal Corollary 7.8 does not by itself establish global separation of measures. The problem input supplies the already established uniqueness modulo constants on the genuine image. With that separation on $\mathcal E^1/\mathbb R$, equal outputs force $I=0$ and hence potentials differing by a constant. This is the given uniqueness conclusion, not a new existence result.

## 6. Direct model computations, including a genuinely irrational atom

The following examples use the local tropical current rule in Wu21's proof of Corollary 5.7, with the mass computed explicitly rather than inferred from the defective toric energy formula.

For a soft maximum $L_\epsilon(z)=\epsilon\log(1+e^{z_1/\epsilon}+\cdots+e^{z_r/\epsilon})$, its gradient maps $\mathbb R^r$ diffeomorphically to the interior of the standard simplex. The change-of-variables formula gives

$$\int_{\mathbb R^r}\det(\nabla^2L_\epsilon)\,dz=1/r!.$$

The superform wedge power $(d'd''L_\epsilon)^r$ has density $r!\det(\nabla^2L_\epsilon)$, so its total tropical mass is one. These measures concentrate at zero as $\epsilon\downarrow0$ by scaling. Likewise the second derivative of $\epsilon\log(1+e^{t/\epsilon})$ has integral one and converges to the atom at zero. An invertible linear coordinate change with matrix $C$ multiplies the tropical top-degree integral by $|\det C|$: the superform has two copies of the coordinate determinant, and integration cancels one. This proves the local atom coefficients used below under the source's current convention.

On $\mathbb A^2$ with $\xi=(1,1)$, put $\rho=\max\{-a,-b\}$ in tropical coordinates and $\phi_s=\max\{-a,s-b\}$, $s>0$. The homogeneous curvature line of $\phi_s$ is $b-a=s$. It intersects the curvature of $\rho^+=\max\{0,-a,-b\}$ only at $(a,b)=(0,s)$. The determinant of the two gradient jumps is one. There is no boundary mass: near a zero coordinate the corresponding term can be discarded, leaving $\phi_s$ locally affine. Thus

$$\operatorname{MA}(\rho)=\delta_{(0,0)},\qquad\operatorname{MA}(\phi_s)=\delta_{(0,s)},\qquad V_\xi=1.$$

The two-term energy formula gives $E(\phi_s)=s/2$. In (1), with $\psi=\rho$, the two bounding integrals are respectively $0$ and $s$. Hence the printed Proposition 7.3 inequality would assert $s/2\le0$, an explicit counterexample to that displayed sign.

Now take $X=\mathbb A^3$, $T=(\mathbb G_m)^3$, and

$$\xi=(1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3),\quad \rho=\max\{-a_1,-a_2/\sqrt2,-a_3/\sqrt3\},$$
$$\phi=\max\{-a_1,1-a_2/\sqrt2,1-a_3/\sqrt3\}.$$

This is a genuine FS function with homogeneous generators $x_1,x_2,x_3$ and parameters $(0,\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$. The lattice-point simplex count gives

$$V_\xi=1/\sqrt6.$$

The square of the homogeneous curvature is supported on the line $a_2=\sqrt2(a_1+1)$, $a_3=\sqrt3(a_1+1)$. Away from this line at most two terms are active, making that square zero. On the line, $\rho=-a_1$, so the radial cut meets it only at

$$w=(0,\sqrt2,\sqrt3)\in K.$$

Near $w$ use coordinates

$$t=-a_1,\quad z_2=1+a_1-a_2/\sqrt2,\quad z_3=1+a_1-a_3/\sqrt3.$$

The reference cut is $\max\{0,t\}$, and $\phi=-a_1+\max\{0,z_2,z_3\}$. The affine common term has zero curvature. The coordinate matrix has determinant of absolute value $1/\sqrt6$, so the preceding smooth calculation proves

$$ (d'd''\phi)^2\wedge d'd''\rho^+=(1/\sqrt6)\delta_w,\qquad\operatorname{MA}_\xi(\phi)=\delta_w.$$

There is no extra coordinate-boundary mass, since at least one of the three terms disappears there and the remaining maximum has curvature rank at most one. The semivaluation $w$ is the monomial valuation giving $x_1$ value zero and $x_2,x_3$ values $\sqrt2,\sqrt3$. It is quasimonomial on the stratum where $x_1$ is a unit; its value group has rational rank two. Since $\sqrt{2/3}$ is irrational, it is not a real rescaling of a divisorial valuation. This gives a genuine irrational fixed-Reeb model output on the correct carrier, with mass exactly one. It is a restricted toric construction and provides no existence theorem for arbitrary measures or general geometry.

## 7. Search for the realization step: precise unresolved passages

The four papers do not furnish a justified transfer establishing the following cone statements. This is a finding about the attempted source applications, not a proof that no future argument or theorem can establish them.

1. **Potential-space compactness/completeness.** Wu24 gives decreasing-net closure, finite-value controls on quasimonomial points, and upper semicontinuity of energy. It does not prove compactness of normalized cone psh functions or strong completeness of the genuine $\mathcal E^1/\mathbb R$. Pointwise boundedness alone gives a limit in a product space; it does not show that the limit is a genuine psh function. BJ22 Theorem 5.11 proves projective compactness through the envelope property, explicitly using upper envelopes of tails. BJ22 Theorem 12.8 identifies that property with strong completeness and surjectivity for a projective ample class. Applying its conclusion to the cone would assume the missing realization.

2. **Envelopes/orthogonality.** Fixed-ray max stability supplies finite maxima, not closure of bounded arbitrary upper envelopes or the orthogonality limit. BJ23 Definition 2.15 requires the actual limit $\int(f-\psi)\operatorname{MA}(\psi)\to0$ for the directed psh tests below every test obstacle. Proposition 2.19 derives uniform differentiation from this assumption. A putative formalism on $K$ would need an ordered space of forms, all positivity axioms, identification of its test psh class with the genuine cone class, and orthogonality. The fixed-ray calculus does not prove that list.

3. **Target integration.** Decreasing FS approximation works by the lemma in Section 4. The general energy-bounded weak convergence needed for maximizing sequences does not follow from it. BJ22 Proposition 9.19 obtains that stronger continuity by uniform approximation of the target by model-MA measures. Its earlier approximation theorem uses uniform differentiation. Invoking Proposition 9.19 on the cone without proving that approximation is circular.

4. **Differentiation and Euler–Lagrange.** Wu24's derivatives along admissible psh segments are sufficient for (1) and (5). They do not give variations in both signs of every dense continuous test. At a hypothetical maximizer $\phi$, admissible segments only give $\int(\psi-\phi)(\operatorname{MA}(\phi)-\mu)\le0$ for psh $\psi$. A maximum on a constrained convex set can have a nonzero outward derivative; for example $-x^2-x$ is maximized at zero on $x\ge0$. BJ22 Theorem 8.5 differentiates an extended energy on arbitrary PL perturbations. Its proof uses projective section-norm relative volumes and mixed masses involving added polarizations. The cone version of that relative-volume comparison is not established here. BJ22 Theorem 9.11 and Corollary 9.12 derive target identification and the Euler–Lagrange equality from that two-sided differentiability, not from concavity alone.

5. **Completion of measures.** BJ23 Theorems 2.23 and 2.26 assume orthogonality, prove density of test outputs, and complete the measure space. The paper expressly does not investigate finite-energy potentials. Even a valid cone application would not identify every completed object with a Wu finite-energy potential. Equation (5) isolates the extra potential realization needed here.

6. **Rational quotient and varying Reeb.** Wu21 Lemmas 5.11–5.12 and Proposition 5.13 identify homogeneous model functions and their measures with quotient functions for primitive rational Reeb fields. A general quotient is normal and can be singular; the supplied BJ22 Theorem 12.9 assumes smoothness. Even for a smooth quotient and a torus larger than the Reeb circle, the actual carrier corresponds to an invariant subset of the quotient, and cone potentials correspond to invariant metrics. Full quotient surjectivity alone is not a proof of preservation of those classes. No quotient transfer or averaging of nonlinear MA is used here. Wu24 Lemmas 2.11/3.2 approximate individual continuous potentials by varying Reeb fields and Proposition 3.3 adds only proportional polarizations. They do not give uniform estimates for target solutions with two changing, nonproportional Reeb fields, nor justify commuting the approximation with finite-energy realization. The irrational toric atom in Section 6 shows why restricting every intermediate measure to divisorial support would also be wrong.

No intrinsic sufficient measure criterion meeting the assignment's exclusions has been established. In particular, variational attainment, existence of an inverse, or a closure defined by unknown finite-energy outputs is not presented as a characterization. The unchanged original P13.2 remains unresolved in this deliverable, including its genuinely general irrational geometry. Uniqueness modulo constants remains the established input on the image.

## 8. Artifacts and reproducibility

The original `input.json` is retained and `input-original.json` is byte-identical. `assignment-original.txt` retains the decoded assignment string exactly, and `task-original.json` retains the unchanged task object. `environment.json` records the existing runtime and TeX tools. `build_provenance.py` verifies the public source hashes and rebuilds the full local literal extracts, selected proof excerpts, and `source-extracts/source-provenance.json`.

`P13.2-paper.tex` is a standalone exposition of these partial arguments; `P13.2-paper.pdf` is its compiled form. `run_checks.py` preserves the actual stdout, stderr, and a separate TeX log for each of two compiler runs, runs exact finite symbolic/rational checks of the signs and combinatorial normalizers, and validates the required artifact schemas and source slices. `checks/check-report.json` records those results. `status.json` has exactly the five requested fields and marks the result incomplete.

Rerun from this directory with `python3 build_provenance.py` and `python3 run_checks.py`. The two actual compiler commands are recorded in `checks/commands.json`; they use the existing `pdflatex` without software installation. No heavy computation was launched. All computational checks concern finite arithmetic, provenance, and document construction. They do not verify the general mathematical arguments, current-theoretic definitions, source theorems, or any solution of P13.2. These are unverified drafts.

This ultimately boils down to understanding the relation between function classes\nwith different polarizations. For example, it will be helpful to understand how PSH(ξ) and\nPSH(ξ ′ ) relate when ξ, ξ ′ are not multiples of each other. We remark that this is a triviality\nin the global case, due to the fact that one can add two FS functions with different polar-\nizations. There is also an analogous statement in the complex analytic setting, see [HL21,\nLemma 6.1].\n   The next step is to try to solve a local NAMA equation. We expect that the general\nframework of Boucksom–Jonsson works in this case as well, but one may need to deal\nwith the subtlety that on a irrationally polarized affine cone, the Monge–Ampère operator\nsends a divisorial norm not to a divisorial measure, but to a quasi-monomial measure, i.e.\na measure supported at genuinely quasimonimial but not divisorial points. This is in fact\none of the main difficulties in this paper already.\n   It is also interesting to understand how much of the local theory would fit into the\nsynthetic approach proposed in [BJ23]. While our setting is slightly different from theirs,\nand this is not the approach we are taking here, the same strategy can be used to define\nthe space of measures of finite energy and form the duality without introducing functions\nof finite energy.\n   We also mention briefly an application of the pluripotential theory in our forthcoming\npreprint. Fix ξ on X.\n  (1) PSH(aξ) = a1 PSH(ξ) for all t ∈ R+ .\n                                               T\n   (2) PSH(ξ) is convex and C 0 (X an \\ {0}, ξ) PSH(ξ) = CPSH(ξ).\n   (3) For any decreasing net (ϕi ) in PSH(ξ) with pointwise limit ϕ, either ϕ ∈ PSH(ξ)\n       or ϕ ≡ −∞.\n\f     SOME NON-ARCHIMEDEAN PLURIPOTENTIAL THEORY ON POLARIZED AFFINE CONES                       15\n\n   (4) Every function in PSH(ξ) is the pointwise limit of a decreasing net in H(ξ).\nProof. In general, pick a decreasing net (ψi ) in CPSH(ξ) with ψi → ψ.\nThen ϕ ≤ ψ ≤ ψi on X qm implies ϕ ≤ ψi on X an and hence ϕ ≤ ψ on X an .               \u0003\n   Finally, we define the Monge–Ampère energy for general psh functions.\nDefinition 5.9.           "literal": "In contrast to E 1 , we prove that both M1 and its strong topology\n                                                             ´     are independent of L.\n   For any two ϕ, ϕ ∈ H, we further have E(ϕ) − E(ϕ ) ≥ (ϕ − ϕ0 ) MA(ϕ), a reflection\n                      0                                 0\n\nof the concavity of E. This precisely means that ϕ computes the supremum defining the\nenergy of MA(ϕ), which thus lies in M1 .\n   The main contribution of the present article can be summarized as follows.\nTheorem A. The Monge–Ampère operator MA : H → M1 admits a unique continuous\nextension MA : E 1 → M1 , where both sides are equipped with the strong topology.\n   It further induces a topological embedding with dense image E 1 /R ,→ M1 , which is onto\nif X is smooth, and either char k = 0 or dim X ≤ 2.\n  Theorem A can be viewed as a trivially valued analogue of the main result of [BBGZ13],\nwhich itself is a version of the celebrated result of Yau [Yau78] and a later version by\nKolodziej [Kol98]. In the non-Archimedean setting, earlier results include [Liu11, BFJ15,\nYZ17].\n\f            GLOBAL PLURIPOTENTIAL THEORY OVER A TRIVIALLY VALUED FIELD                       5\n\n  Theorem A actually brings together several main steps, of various flavors, that we now",

          "literal": "5.2. The envelope property and unibranch varieties. In the rest of §4 we assume that\nX is irreducible unless stated otherwise. (See Remark 5.15.)\nDefinition 5.8. We say that a class θ ∈ N1 (X) has the envelope property if, for any\nbounded-above family (ϕi ) in PSH(θ), the usc upper envelope sup?i ϕi is θ-psh.\n   In the complex analytic case, it is a basic fact that psh functions on domains in Cn\nsatisfy the analogue of the envelope property. As a consequence, θ-psh functions satisfy the\nenvelope property for any projective complex manifold X and any closed (1, 1)-form θ. More\ngenerally, the latter property holds when X is unibranch (i.e. locally analytically irreducible),\ncf. [Dem85, Théorème 1.7], but fails in general, for the same reason as Theorem 5.12 below.\n   With our global definition of θ-psh functions, the envelope property turns out to be\nespecially delicate. The purpose of what follows is to explore various implications, and\nestablish it in an important special case. We first observe:\nLemma 5.9. Assume that θ ∈ N1 (X) can be written as the limit of classes θj ≥ θ that\nsatisfy the envelope property. Then θ has the envelope property as well.\n\f58                       SÉBASTIEN BOUCKSOM AND MATTIAS JONSSON\n\nProof. Pick a bounded-above family (ϕi ) in PSH(θ). Since θ ≤ θj , we have PSH(θ) ⊂\nPSH(θj ). Thus sup?i ϕi is θj -psh for all j, and hence θ-psh, by Theorem 4.5.    \u0003\nCorollary 5.10. If the continuity property holds for all ω ∈ Amp(X), then it holds for all\nθ ∈ Nef(X).\n  We next prove that the envelope property is equivalent to the analogue of a basic com-\npactness property in the complex analytic case.\nTheorem 5.11. For any θ ∈ N1 (X), the following properties are equivalent:\n    (i) the envelope property holds for θ;\n   (ii) the space PSHsup (θ) := {ϕ ∈ PSH(θ) | sup ϕ = 0} is compact;\n  (iii) every bounded-above, increasing net (ϕj ) in PSH(θ) converges in PSH(θ).\nProof. Assume (i), and pick a net (ϕi ) in PSHsup (θ). By Proposition 4.38, (ϕi (v)) is a\nbounded net in R for each v ∈ X div . By Tychonoff’s theorem, after passing to a subnet,\nwe may thus assume that (ϕi ) converges pointwise on X div to a function ϕ : X div → R,\nand it suffices to show that ϕ extends to a function in PSH(θ) (necessarily unique, by\nCorollary 4.23). By (i), ψi := sup?j≥i ϕj is θ-psh for each i. The net (ψi ) is further decreasing,\nand its pointwise limit ψ := limi ψi is thus either θ-psh, or identically −∞, by Theorem 4.5.\nNow Theorem 5.6 implies that ψi = supj≥i ϕj on X div . # Complete actual public primary text: 2406.13684v1

                                                SOME NON-ARCHIMEDEAN PLURIPOTENTIAL THEORY ON
                                                            POLARIZED AFFINE CONES

                                                                                      YUEQIAO WU
arXiv:2406.13684v1 [math.AG] 19 Jun 2024




                                                  Abstract. We undertake a preliminary step towards studying non-Archimedean pluripo-
                                                  tential theory on polarized affine cones over a trivially valued field. We study plurisub-
                                                  harmonic functions and the Monge–Ampère operator defined on the finite energy class,
                                                  partially generalizing a result of Boucksom–Jonsson on projective varieties.




                                                                                        Contents
                                             1. Introduction                                                                                    1
                                             2. Preliminaries                                                                                   4
                                             3. Continuous plurisubharmonic functions                                                           7
                                             4. Energy functionals on continuous plurisubharmonic functions                                    10
                                             5. General plurisubharmonic functions                                                             14
                                             6. Functions of finite energy and mixed MA measures                                               18
                                             7. Measures of finite energy                                                                      22
                                             References                                                                                        25



                                                                                   1. Introduction
                                              Throughout the paper, we work over a trivially valued algebraically closed field of char-
                                           acteristic zero. The goal of this paper is to serve as a starting point to understand pluripo-
                                           tential theory on Berkovich analytifications of polarized affine cones initiated in [Wu22],
                                           following the framework of Boucksom–Jonsson [BJ22]. While we do not generalize all of
                                           the global theory in loc.cit. for now, we aim to present what can be carried out in our
                                           setting, describe the key obstacles, and provide sufficient background for an application to
                                           local K-stability.
                                              Complex pluripotential theory has played an important role towards solving the complex
                                           Monge–Ampère equation via a variational approach in [BBGZ13]. Inspired by this, the
                                           variational approach to the Yau–Tian–Donaldson (YTD) conjecture for log Fano varieties
                                           (see [BBJ21, Li22]) motivates a systematic study of global non-Archimedean pluripotential
                                           theory over trivially valued fields. As developed by Boucksom–Jonsson in [BJ22], the
                                           global theory provides a variational approach to the solution of a non-Archimedean Monge–
                                           Ampère equation over trivially valued fields. This is analogous to a sequence of celebrated
                                           results on Monge–Ampère equations in different settings over the past few decades, dating
                                           back to Yau’s theorem [Yau78] solving the Calabi conjecture; and more recently a non-
                                           Archimedean version of that over discretely valued fields proved in [BFJ15].
                                              In this paper, we focus on studying the non-Archimedean pluripotential theory on affine
                                           cones over projective varieties. We briefly explain the local setting that we are working in.
                                           Let (X = Spec R, T, ξ) be a polarized affine cone, i.e. X is a normal affine variety, T is a
                                           torus of automorphisms with a unique fixed point o ∈ X with ideal m, and ξ is a vector
                                                                                              1
2                                        YUEQIAO WU

generating a subtorus of T and acting with positive weights. Each ξ gives a T-invariant
quasi-monomial valuation vξ on X centered at o, and it is divisorial if and only if ξ generates
a Gm action. In the case when vξ is divisorial, one can realize X as the affine cone over
some polarized pair. As originally introduced in [CS18], building on the ideas of [MSY08],
there is a local K-stability theory for polarized affine cones, which agrees with the one for
polarized pairs when vξ is divisorial. Moreover, it is a continuous extension of the global
K-stability theory in the sense that the Futaki invariant in loc.cit. depends continuously on
ξ. Relevant YTD type results have been obtained for log Fano cone singularities, that is,
Q-Gorenstein polarized affine cones with klt singularities, see [CS19, LX18, LWX21, Li21].
This also motivates the study of NA pluripotential theory on polarized affine cones.
   We now briefly explain the key ideas and difficulties in the local case. In the global
setting, the theory of Boucksom–Jonsson relies on the intersection theory and positivity
results provided by the geometry of projective varieties. From this point of view, one
might hope the existing local intersection theory, for example Hilbert–Samuel multiplici-
ties, would lead to a local pluripotential theory in our setting. This is in fact the direction
that has been extensively studied in [BLQ24], but will not be the point of view taken here.
Philosophically, the local setting we are working in is different from the traditional one in
algebraic geometry and commutative algebra, in the sense that the Reeb field provides a
polarization in addition to the information on the singularity of the cone point. Neverthe-
less, the theory by Chambert–Loir and Ducros (see [CLD12]) we are relying on has a more
analytic and local nature. Thus one would hope that a similar local non-Archimedean
pluripotential theory can be developed, paralleling the global story.
                                             L
Main result. Let (X = Spec R = Spec α Rα , ξ) be a polarized affine cone described
before, and write X an for the Berkovich analytification of X with respect to the trivial
valuation on k. This consists of all semivaluations on X extending the trivial valuation on
k, equipped with the topology of pointwise convergence. Motivated by Sasakian geometry,
the NA link is defined to be
                                X0 := {v ∈ X an | v(m) = 0}.
This is a compact analytic domain in X an , independent of the polarization ξ. While we
mostly work with punctured cone X an \ {o} when defining different classes of functions,
the cone structure on X allows us to think of them as functions on X0 , via certain ξ-
equivariance. More importantly, the Monge–Ampère measures will always be supported
on X0 , and it will be convenient to deal with convergence theory on X0 .
  Analogous to the Fubini–Study metrics studied in [BJ22], the class H(ξ) of Fubini–Study
functions was introduced in [Wu22] as continuous functions ϕ : X an \ {o} → R of the form
                                             log |fαj | + λj
                                  ϕ = max{                   }
                                        αj       hξ, αj i
for a finite set of fαj ∈ Rαj generating an m-primary ideal. In particular, we always have
a canonical reference function ϕξ , where all λj = 0 and fαj ’s generate the maximal ideal
m. One can alternatively identify X0 with the set {ϕξ = 0}, analogous to the construction
in Sasakian geometry, see e.g. [BG08]. Unlike FS metrics, FS functions behave differently
when ξ is irrational. For example, adding two FS functions does not give a FS function in
general. A more subtle difference is that the Monge–Ampère measures will have support
on quasi-monomial valuations instead of just divisorial valuations. To get around this
issue, for a fixed polarization ξ, we are going to enlarge the space of FS functions first
by passing to its closure in the space of ξ-equivariant continuous functions on X an , which
we call the space of continuous psh functions CPSH(ξ). Following the same pattern as in
     SOME NON-ARCHIMEDEAN PLURIPOTENTIAL THEORY ON POLARIZED AFFINE CONES                       3

the complex analytic and global non-Archimedean theory, we define a psh function to be
an upper-semicontinuous (usc) function that is the pointwise limit of a decreasing net of
continuous psh functions, the Monge–Ampère energy defined in [Wu22] naturally extends
to a functional E : PSH(ξ) → R ∪ {−∞} on psh functions. The finite energy class, which
in particular contains CPSH(ξ), is defined to be
                            E 1 (ξ) := {ϕ ∈ PSH(ξ) : E(ϕ) > −∞}.
One can dually define the energy E∨ : M(X0 ) → [0, +∞] from the space of Radon proba-
bility measures on X supported on X0 via

and the space of measures of finite energy by
                           M1 (ξ) := {µ ∈ M(X0 ) : E∨ (µ) < +∞}.
There are also natural quasi-pseudometrics I on E 1 (ξ) and dually I∨ on M1 (ξ). We note
that by construction one has MA(H(ξ)) ⊂ M1 (ξ). As a local analog of [BJ22, Theorem
7.14], our main result extends the Monge–Ampère operator from H(ξ) to E 1 (ξ):
Theorem 1.1. There is a unique extension of the Monge–Ampère operator MA : H(ξ) →
M1 (ξ) to MA : (E 1 (ξ), I) → (M1 (ξ), I∨ ), which is continuous along decreasing nets in
E 1 (ξ), and bi-Lipschitz with respect to I and I∨ .
Outlook and relation to other works. A key missing ingredient that prevents us from
generalizing Boucksom–Jonsson’s result on studying the image of the Monge–Ampère op-
erator in M1 in full generality is the uniform differentiability result, see [BJ22, Theorem
8.5]. This ultimately boils down to understanding the relation between function classes
with different polarizations. For example, it will be helpful to understand how PSH(ξ) and
PSH(ξ ′ ) relate when ξ, ξ ′ are not multiples of each other. We remark that this is a triviality
in the global case, due to the fact that one can add two FS functions with different polar-
izations. There is also an analogous statement in the complex analytic setting, see [HL21,
Lemma 6.1].
   The next step is to try to solve a local NAMA equation. We expect that the general
framework of Boucksom–Jonsson works in this case as well, but one may need to deal
with the subtlety that on a irrationally polarized affine cone, the Monge–Ampère operator
sends a divisorial norm not to a divisorial measure, but to a quasi-monomial measure, i.e.
a measure supported at genuinely quasimonimial but not divisorial points. This is in fact
one of the main difficulties in this paper already.
   It is also interesting to understand how much of the local theory would fit into the
synthetic approach proposed in [BJ23]. While our setting is slightly different from theirs,
and this is not the approach we are taking here, the same strategy can be used to define
the space of measures of finite energy and form the duality without introducing functions
of finite energy.
   We also mention briefly an application of the pluripotential theory in our forthcoming
preprint. Specifically, the Monge–Ampère operator defined on the finite energy class gives
an alternative characterization of the Monge–Ampère energy using measures of finite en-
ergy, see Proposition 7.3. Using the duality of energy of psh functions and measures, and
following the ideas of [BBJ21], one can show that to test K-semistability of log Fano cone
singularities, it suffices to test special test configurations. This is a local analog of [LX14].

Structure of the paper. In Section 2, we recall basic definitions and notation, and results
in [Wu22] on the Monge–Ampère operator defined on test configurations, or equivalently
the space of FS functions. We extend the theory to continuous psh functions in Section 3
and Section 4. Section 5 is devoted to the theory of general psh functions. The first part
of the main theorem is proved in Section 6. Finally in Section 7, we introduce the space of
measures of finite energy and complete the proof of the main theorem.

                     3. Continuous plurisubharmonic functions
   In this section we introduce a broader class of plurisubharmonic (psh) functions than
FS functions. Unlike the global case, where the sum of two FS functions is still a FS
function; more precisely, one can add two metrics on two line bundles L1 , L2 respectively
to get a new metric on L1 + L2 , FS functions are more rigid in the local case. First, it
is not clear what it means to add two FS functions with non-proportional polarizations.
While we believe there is some intepretation that can be made in this situation, this shall
not be our focus here. Thus in the sequel, we will often fix a polarization ξ. Second, when
ξ is irrational, the sum of two FS functions with the same polarization may not be a FS
function anymore. Thus we need to start with a larger class: the class of continuous psh
functions.
Definition 3.1. The space of continuous ξ-psh functions CPSH(ξ) is the closure of H(ξ)
in the space C 0 (X an , ξ) of continuous ξ-equivariant functions with topology given by local
uniform convergence.
   It follows directly from the definition that this class of functions are indeed continuous
and psh-approachable in the sense of Chambert–Loir and Ducros. The following lemma
gives a more concrete description of cpsh functions.

                              5. General plurisubharmonic functions
  In this section, we extend our class of psh functions even further to allow only upper-
semicontinuous (usc) functions. We also extend the Monge-Ampère operator to this class.
The main goal is to show that this extended Monge-Ampère energy still has nice continuity
properties.
Definition 5.1. We call ϕ : X an → R ∪ {−∞} a ξ-plurisubharmonic (ξ-psh) function on
(X an ; ξ) if ϕ is a pointwise limit of a decreasing net (ϕi ) in CPSH(ξ), and ϕ 6≡ −∞. We
denote by PSH(ξ) the set of ξ-psh functions on X an .
Proposition 5.2. Fix ξ on X.
  (1) PSH(aξ) = a1 PSH(ξ) for all t ∈ R+ .
                                               T
   (2) PSH(ξ) is convex and C 0 (X an \ {0}, ξ) PSH(ξ) = CPSH(ξ).
   (3) For any decreasing net (ϕi ) in PSH(ξ) with pointwise limit ϕ, either ϕ ∈ PSH(ξ)
       or ϕ ≡ −∞.
     SOME NON-ARCHIMEDEAN PLURIPOTENTIAL THEORY ON POLARIZED AFFINE CONES                       15

   (4) Every function in PSH(ξ) is the pointwise limit of a decreasing net in H(ξ).
Proof. (1) and first assertion of (2) follow from analogous result on continous psh functions.
It is clear that CPSH(ξ) ⊆ C 0 (X an \ {o}, ξ) ∩ PSH(ξ). Let ϕ ∈ PSH(ξ) be a function
that is also continuous on X an \ {o}. Then by definition, there is a decreasing sequence
ϕi ∈ CPSH(ξ) converging pointwise to ϕ. Then on each compact subset K ⊂ X an \{o}, the
convergence is uniform by Dini’s lemma. Hence C 0 (X an \ {o}, ξ) ∩ PSH(ξ) = CPSH(ξ). (3)
and (4) are consequences of [BJ22, Lemma 4.6] with K = X0 , Fe = CPSH(ξ), F = H(ξ). 

Theorem 5.8. Given ϕ, ψ ∈ PSH(ξ), ϕ ≤ ψ on X an if and only if ϕ ≤ ψ on X qm . In
particular, the topology of PSH(ξ) is Hausdorff.
Proof. If ψ ∈ FS(ξ), then this is a consequence of Lemma 5.5. Arguing as in the previous
corollary, this is true for ψ ∈ CPSH(ξ) since CPSH(ξ) is the closure of FS(ξ) under local
uniform convergence. In general, pick a decreasing net (ψi ) in CPSH(ξ) with ψi → ψ.
Then ϕ ≤ ψ ≤ ψi on X qm implies ϕ ≤ ψi on X an and hence ϕ ≤ ψ on X an .               
   Finally, we define the Monge–Ampère energy for general psh functions.
Definition 5.9. Let ϕ ∈ PSH(ξ). The Monge–Ampère energy for ϕ is defined as
                     E(ϕ) = Eξ (ϕ) := inf{E(ψ) : ϕ ≤ ψ, ψ ∈ CPSH(ξ)}.
18                                                YUEQIAO WU

  In view of Proposition 5.2, we can also take ψ ∈ H(ξ) in the above definition. The next
proposition summarizes the main properties of E.
Proposition 5.10. The Monge-Ampère energy E : PSH(ξ) → R ∪ {−∞} satisfies the
following properties:
    (1) E is non-decreasing.
    (2) E(ϕ + c) = E(ϕ) + c.
    (3) E is upper semicontinuous.
    (4) E is continuous along decreasing nets.
    (5) E is concave.
Proof. The first two assertions are obvious, and (4) is a consequence of upper semicontinuity
and monotonicity. (5) follows from (4) and the fact that E is concave on CPSH(ξ). It
remains to show upper semicontinuity. The proof goes along the same lines as in [BJ22,
Theorem 7.1]. Suppose that ϕ ∈ PSH(ξ) and t ∈ R satisfies E(ϕ) < t. We can choose
ψ ∈ CPSH(ξ) and ε > 0 such that ϕ ≤ ψ and E(ψ) < t−ε. By Proposition 5.7, we can find
an open neighborhood U of ϕ in PSH(ξ) such that ϕ′ ≤ ψ + ε for all ϕ′ ∈ U . Monotonicity
then gives
                              E(ϕ′ ) ≤ E(ψ + ε) = t − ε + ε = t,
for all ϕ′ ∈ U . This proves (3).                                                          

                   6. Functions of finite energy and mixed MA measures
  As suggested by the work of Berman–Boucksom–Jonsson [BBJ21], the non-Archimedean
version of the finite energy class can play an important role in geometric applications. In
the local case, we have a similar theory of functions of finite energy.
Definition 6.1. We say ϕ ∈ PSH(ξ) is a function of finite energy if E(ϕ) > −∞. The
space of functions of finite energy is denoted by E 1 (ξ).
     The following is a direct consequence of Proposition 5.10.
Proposition 6.2. The space E 1 (ξ) satisfies the following:
   (1) If ϕ ∈ E 1 (ξ) and c ∈ R, then ϕ + c ∈ E 1 (ξ).
   (2) E 1 (ξ) is convex.
   (3) If ϕ ≤ ψ and ϕ ∈ E 1 (ξ), then ψ ∈ E 1 (ξ).
   (4) CPSH(ξ) ⊂ E 1 (ξ).

# Complete actual public primary text: 2106.13395v2

                                           VOLUME AND MONGE-AMPÈRE ENERGY ON POLARIZED AFFINE
                                                               VARIETIES
arXiv:2106.13395v2 [math.AG] 14 Feb 2022




                                                                                      YUEQIAO WU


                                                  Abstract. Let (X, ξ) be a polarized affine variety, i.e. an affine variety X with a
                                                  (possibly irrational) Reeb vector field ξ. We define the volume of a filtration of the
                                                  coordinate ring of X in terms of the asymptotics of the average of jumping numbers.
                                                  When the filtration is finitely generated, it induces a Fubini-Study function ϕ on the
                                                  Berkovich analytification of X. In this case, we define the Monge-Ampère energy for ϕ
                                                  using the theory of forms and currents on Berkovich spaces developed by Chambert-Loir
                                                  and Ducros, and show that it agrees with the volume of the filtration. In the special case
                                                  when the filtration comes from a test configuration, we recover the functional defined by
                                                  Collins-Székelyhidi and Li-Xu.




                                                                                        Contents
                                             1. Introduction                                                                                    1
                                             2. Background                                                                                      4
                                             3. Filtrations and Okounkov bodies                                                                 8
                                             4. Monge-Ampère energy of a test configuration                                                   15
                                             5. Monge-Ampère energy of Fubini-Study functions                                                 17
                                             6. The toric case                                                                                 26
                                             References                                                                                        28



                                                                                   1. Introduction
                                              We work over an algebraically closed field K of characteristic zero. Let V be a Fano
                                           variety. The Yau-Tian-Donaldson conjecture, proved in [CDS15, Tia15], and more recently
                                           using a variational approach in [BBJ21, Li21, LXZ21], states that V admits a weak Kähler-
                                           Einstein metric if and only if it’s K-polystable. This was generalized in [CS19] to Kähler
                                           cones, relating the existence of a Ricci flat Kähler cone metric to K-stability. As part of
                                           the variational approach, a Monge-Ampère energy was introduced for a test configuration,
                                           and later an algebraic formulation was given in [LX18, LWX21] computing the limit slope
                                           of the Monge-Ampère energy.
                                              Let (X = Spec R, T, ξ) be a polarized affine variety, i.e. X is a normal affine variety,
                                           T is a torus of automorphisms with a unique fixed point 0 ∈ X with ideal m, and ξ is a
                                           vector field generating a subtorus of T and acting with positive weights.LWe will usually
                                           omit T and write (X, ξ) to mean the polarized affine variety. Let R = α∈Λ Rα be the
                                           weight decomposition of R with respect to T, where Λ = {α ∈ Hom(T, Gm ) : Rα 6= 0}.
                                           Let n be the dimension of X.

up to a dimensional constant C(n).
   The main strategy is to first prove the case when ξ is rational. In this case, write
X = C(V, L) as the cone of a polarized pair (V, L). The test configuration for (X, ξ)
corresponds to the cone of an ample test configuration (V, L) for (V, L). This gives us
a Fubini-Study metric φ on Lan . We show that E NA (ϕ) = E NA (φ). The general result
then follows from approximating ξ by rational ones. We anticipate that this energy be
extended to a bigger class of functions, e.g. the finite energy class, and other related
non-Archimedean functionals be defined in our future work.
   Finally, we look at the toric case. When X is an affine toric variety of dimension n
associated to a cone σ ⊂ NR , ξ can be thought of as a vector in the interior of σ, and

Organization. This paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we briefly recall notions
of valuations, test configurations, Berkovich analytifications, and the theory of forms and
currents on Berkovich spaces. In section 3, we construct a local analog of Okounkov
bodies associated to a filtration, using which we define the volume of a filtration. A first
formulation of the NA Monge-Ampère energy is given in section 4, and we show that it
computes the limit slope of the Monge-Ampère energy defined in [CS19] if the filtration
comes from a test configuration. Section 5 is devoted to another formulation of the energy
using forms and currents on Berkovich spaces, and Theorem 1.1 is proved here. Finally,
section 6 studies similar formulations in the toric case.

also grateful to the anonymous referee for very helpful comments.

                                     2. Background
2.1. Polarized affine varieties and test configurations. We work over an algebraically
closed field K of characteristic 0. Let X = Spec R be an n-dimensional normal affine va-
riety(not necessarily irreducible).
   Let T be a split torus acting on X. Set N := Hom(Gm , T) to be the co-weight lattice,
and let M be the dual lattice. We then have a weight decomposition on R:
                                            M
                                        R=     Rα ,
                                                α∈Λ
where Λ := {α ∈ M : Rα 6= 0}. A T action on X is good if has a unique fixed point 0 ∈ X
that is in the closure of all T-orbits and R0 = K. In this paper, we will always assume
that the action is good.
  We now set up some definitions introduced in [CS19].
Definition 2.1. The Reeb cone of X with respect to the T action is
                    C := {ξ ∈ NR := N ⊗ R : hξ, αi > 0, ∀α ∈ Λ \ {0}}
A vector ξ ∈ C is called a Reeb vector field.
         VOLUME AND MONGE-AMPÈRE ENERGY ON POLARIZED AFFINE VARIETIES                      5

Definition 2.2. A polarized affine variety is a triple (X, T, ξ) such that T is a good action
on X, and ξ is a Reeb vector field. Further, we call a polarized affine variety (X, T, ξ)
quasi-regular if ξ is rational, i.e., ξ ∈ NQ . Otherwise, it’s said to be irregular.
Remark 2.3. This is more commonly known as a log Fano cone singularity when X
has klt singularities. We adopt a different name here since we do not assume X has klt
singularities.
Definition 2.4. For a Reeb vector field ξ ∈ C, its volume is defined to be

  The above limit exists by [CS18].
Definition 2.5. A (real) semivaluation v on X is a map v : R → R ∪ {∞} such that
   (1) v(f + g) ≥ min{v(f ), v(g)}, ∀f, g ∈ R;
   (2) v(f g) = v(f ) + v(g), ∀f, g ∈ R;
   (3) v(0) = ∞;
   (4) v|K∗ = 0.
A valuation v is a semivaluation such that v(f ) = ∞ if and only if f = 0.

   We remark that ξ plays the role of a polarization (see [CS18]). Indeed, when ξ is
rational, say ξ ∈ 1l N , it generates a Gm action. So one can think of X \ {0} as the
complement of the zero section in the total space of an ample orbiline bundle over some
orbifold. In algebro-geometric terms, X \ {0} is a Seifert Gm -bundle over a projective
variety V = Proj R. It’s shown in [Kol] that the coordinate ring R with the new grading
induced by the ξ action can be viewed as the section ring of some Q-line bundle L on V :

   (1) X = Spec R is an affine variety

  We shall also need the notion of psh functions on Berkovich spaces. The following
definitions and facts are taken from [CLD12].
Definition 2.10. A continuous function u on Z is plurisubharmonic (psh) if d′ d′′ u ≥ 0,
i.e., hu, d′ d′′ αi ≥ 0 for all compactly supported smooth (n − 1, n − 1)-forms α on Z.
   We say u is psh-approachable if any point in Z has an open neighborhood U on which
u is the uniform limit of smooth psh functions.
Example 2.11. Let u be a function on Z. Assume that for any z ∈ Z, there is an open
neighborhood U of z and a moment map f on U such that u|U = f ∗ v for some convex
function v on some polyhedron ftrop (U ). Then u is psh-approachable.

# Complete actual public primary text: 1801.08229v4

                                           GLOBAL PLURIPOTENTIAL THEORY OVER A TRIVIALLY VALUED
                                                                   FIELD

                                                                   SÉBASTIEN BOUCKSOM AND MATTIAS JONSSON
arXiv:1801.08229v4 [math.AG] 22 Mar 2022




                                                  Dedicated to Ahmed Zeriahi for all his contributions to complex analysis and geometry


                                                Abstract. We develop global pluripotential theory in the setting of Berkovich geometry
                                                over a trivially valued field. Specifically, we define and study functions and measures of
                                                finite energy and the non-Archimedean Monge–Ampère operator on any (possibly reducible)
                                                projective variety. We also investigate the topology of the space of valuations of linear
                                                growth, and the behavior of psh functions thereon.
                                                   Nous développons une théorie du pluripotentiel global dans le contexte de la géométrie de
                                                Berkovich sur un corps trivialement valué. Plus précisément, nous définissons et étudions
                                                des fonctions et mesures d’énergie finie et un opérateur de Monge–Ampère non-archimédien
                                                sur toute variéte projective (éventuellement réductible). Nous explorons également la topolo-
                                                gie de l’espace des valuations à croissance linéaire, et le comportement des fonctions psh
                                                sur celui-ci.

2                        SÉBASTIEN BOUCKSOM AND MATTIAS JONSSON

                                        Introduction
   The main purpose of the present paper is to lay the foundations of pluripotential theory
in the setting of Berkovich geometry over a trivially valued field, paralleling as much as
possible the known theory in the complex analytic case.
   Pluripotential theory is a crucial tool in complex analysis and geometry, and A. Zeriahi has
been a central protagonist in the story of its development. For an excellent introduction, see
the book by V. Guedj and A. Zeriahi [GZ17]. This theory lies at the heart of the variational
approach to complex Monge–Ampère equations [BBGZ13], which proved particularly fruitful
in relation to Kähler–Einstein metrics, and ultimately led to a new proof of the Yau–Tian–
Donaldson (YTD) conjecture for Fano manifolds [BBJ21], later generalized to (log terminal)
Fano varieties [LTW19, Li19].
   There are several reasons for developing a corresponding theory over a trivially valued
field, that is, any field equipped with the trivial (non-Archimedean) valuation. First, the
Berkovich approach to non-Archimedean geometry is the one closest to the complex ana-
lytic intuition, and it is natural to see to what extent the complex analytic theory admits
a counterpart in the setting of Berkovich spaces. Second, Berkovich spaces over a triv-
ially or discretely valued field can often be used to study degenerations in complex geome-
try [FJ05a, FJ05b, FJ07, FJ11, BoJ17, BHJ19, Shi19], and such degenerations are central
to the variational approach to the YTD conjecture [BBJ21, Li20], through the notion of
geodesic rays.
   The thrust of the YTD conjecture is to relate the existence of a solution to a non-linear
PDE to an algebro-geometric condition known as K-stability, which has recently also come
to play a key role in the study of moduli spaces, especially for Fano varieties. [ABHX20,
BHLX21, BLX19, LXZ21, XZ20]. The relation of K-stability with spaces of valuations and
non-Archimedean geometry over trivially valued fields, originally pointed out in [BHJ17], is
one major motivation to endeavor the present study, and will be further exploited in the
companion papers [BoJ21, BoJ22].
   K-stability of a polarized projective variety (X, L) over an algebraically closed field k is a
condition phrased in terms of Gm -equivariant degenerations (X , L) → A1 of (X, L) known
as test configurations [Don02]. Our basic proposal, which goes back to [BHJ17], consists in
interpreting (X , L) in terms of a piecewise linear function ϕL on the Berkovich analytification
X an with respect to the trivial absolute value on the ground field k. To readers familiar with
non-Archimedean geometry, this will sound very natural indeed: the base change of a test
configuration (X , L) by Spec k[[$]] → A1 = Spec k[$] provides a model for the base change
(XK , LK ) to the non-Archimedean field K = k(($)), and hence a model/PL metric on the
Berkovich analytification Lan           an
                               K → XK . This metric can further be canonically identified
with a PL function on XK , thanks to the reference metric on Lan
                            an
                                                                      K induced by the trivial
model, and ϕL is simply the restriction of this function to X an ,→ XK an , the embedding being

realized by Gauss extension.
   While this point of view was basically the one adopted in a previous version of this
article [BoJ18a], we have tried here to take a more elementary and self-contained approach,
avoiding for the most part any explicit reference to general Berkovich geometry—which
accounts in part for the length of the present article.
               GLOBAL PLURIPOTENTIAL THEORY OVER A TRIVIALLY VALUED FIELD                                  3

Functions and measures of finite energy. Let k be an arbitrary algebraically closed
field, and X an irreducible1 projective variety over k, with function field k(X). In order to
describe more precisely our main results, recall first that the Berkovich analytification X an
of X with respect to the trivial valuation on k is a compactification of the space X val of
valuations v : k(X)× → R, trivial on k, endowed with the topology of pointwise convergence.
Points of X an can be understood as semivaluations v on X, i.e. valuations v ∈ Y val for some
subvariety Y ⊂ X. The set X div ⊂ X val of divisorial valuations, which are attached to
prime divisors over X, is dense in X an .
   For every v ∈ X an and every section s ∈ H0 (X, mL), m ∈ N, we can make sense of
v(s) ∈ [0, +∞] by trivializing L at the center of v. Setting |s|(v) := exp(−v(s)) defines a
continuous function |s| : X an → [0, 1], and the topology of X an is in fact defined by the set
of such functions. Building on these, we introduce the following classes of functions on X an :
      • Fubini–Study functions for L are continuous functions ϕ : X an → R of the form

                                     ϕ = m−1 max{log |si | + λi },
                                                   i

         where (si ) is a finite set in H0 (X, mL) without common zeroes and λi ∈ Q. This
         defines a subset H = H(L) of C0 (X) := C0 (X an , R), and we show that the map
         (X , L) 7→ ϕL alluded to above sets up a 1–1 correspondence between H(L) and the
         set of ample, integrally closed test configurations (X , L) for (X, L) (see §1.4 for the
         definition when X is not normal).
      • piecewise linear (PL) functions on X an are elements of the Q-linear subspace PL(X)
        of C0 (X) spanned by H = H(L); this subspace turns out to be independent of L,
        and is dense in C0 (X). In the present setting, PL functions play the role of smooth
        functions from the complex analytic case. It is proved in Appendix A that PL
        functions are induced by usual piecewise linear functions on dual complexes of snc
        test configurations, when X is smooth and char k = 0.
      • L-psh functions are usc functions ϕ : X an → R∪{−∞}, not identically −∞, that can
        be obtained as limits of decreasing nets in H(L). The set PSH = PSH(L) of L-psh
        functions is stable under addition of a real constant, finite maxima, decreasing limits,
        and is the smallest such class of functions that contains all functions of the form
        m−1 log |s|, s ∈ H0 (X, mL) \ {0}. It follows from Dini’s lemma that C0 (X) ∩ PSH
        is the closure of H in the topology of uniform convergence. We prove that the
        restriction of an L-psh function ϕ to X div is finite-valued, and determines ϕ. We
        endow the set PSH with the topology of pointwise convergence on X div .
In the main body of the text, we actually work with ω-psh functions, where ω ∈ N1 (X) is
any (real) ample (and sometimes even arbitrary) numerical class on X. However, here we
will stick to the above setting, for simplicity.
   As in [BHJ17], the Monge–Ampère energy E : H → R is defined on ϕ ∈ H as the normal-
ized intersection number (or height)

 The envelope property. In the complex analytic case, it is a basic fact that the (usc) envelope
sup?i ϕi of any family (ϕi ) of psh functions on a (smooth) complex manifold remains psh.
This remains true for psh functions on any complex space that is locally irreducible in the
analytic topology, but fails in general without this assumption. In our setting, we say that
L has the envelope property if the previous property holds. We prove that it implies that
X is unibranch, which means that the normalization ν : X ν → X is a homeomorphism (in
the Zariski topology), and is equivalent to X being locally analytically irreducible in the
complex case. Conversely, we conjecture that the envelope property holds as soon as X is
unibranch (e.g. normal), and prove that it holds when X is smooth and either char k = 0 or
dim X ≤ 2, by adapting arguments from [BFJ16, GJKM17].
  We further show that the envelope property is equivalent to the analogues of several
fundamental known facts in the complex analytic case:
       • weak compactness of PSH /R;
       • completeness of E 1 /R with respect to the quasi-metric I;
       • surjectivity of MA : E 1 → M1 .
  It is also equivalent to the property that for any ϕ ∈ C0 (X), the psh envelope
                                 P(ϕ) := sup{ψ ∈ PSH, ψ ≤ ϕ}
is continuous (or, equivalently, L-psh).

Valuations of linear growth. The results mentioned so far have been quite similar to
the complex analytic picture; we now focus on some aspects that are specific to the non-
Archimedean setting. We say that a subset E ⊂ X an is pluripolar if E ⊂ {ϕ = −∞}
for some ϕ ∈ PSH, this condition being independent of L. As opposed to the complex
analytic case, a point v ∈ X an can be nonpluripolar. This is for instance the case for
a divisorial valuation v ∈ X div , and we show more generally that a point v ∈ X an is
             GLOBAL PLURIPOTENTIAL THEORY OVER A TRIVIALLY VALUED FIELD                          7

nonpluripolar iff v is a valuation of linear growth in the sense of [BKMS15], i.e. v(s) ≤ Cm
for all s ∈ H0 (X, mL) \ {0}, for a uniform constant C > 0.
   We turn the set X lin of valuations of linear growth into a metric space—later shown to
be complete—by setting
             d∞ (v, w) := sup m−1 |v(s) − w(s)| | m ≥ 1, s ∈ H0 (X, mL) \ {0} .

We refer to the metric space topology of X lin as the strong topology, the weak topology being
the one inherited from X an . This interacts nicely with the space M1 , as follows:
Theorem B. A point v ∈ X an lies in X lin iff the Dirac mass δv lies in M1 . Furthermore,
the map v 7→ δv defines a closed embedding X lin ,→ M1 , with respect to both the weak and
the strong topologies (on both sides), onto the set of extremal points of the convex set M1 .
  Thus a net (vi ) in X lin converges strongly to v iff vi → v weakly and E∨ (δvi ) → E∨ (δv ).
As we shall see in the companion paper [BoJ21], the energy E∨ (δv ) coincides with the
expected vanishing order S(v) [FO16, BlJ20], an invariant that appears in the definition of
the stability threshold (or δ-invariant) that has come to play a key role in recent works on
K-stability of Fano varieties, such as [BX19, BLZ19] to name just a few.
  Our final main result analyzes the behavior of L-psh functions on X lin .
Theorem C. Pick any L-psh function ϕ. Then:
